passage: In a classroom in Seville, Senora Ruiz held up a picture of a snail. "Who knows what this is?" Javier, five, bounced off his chair. "CARACOL! I know! I know!" Valentina kept her hand high and still, though her fingers wiggled. Senora Ruiz smiled at Javier. "Back on your chair, please. Hands up." Javier flopped down, arms folded, and kicked the table leg. "Not fair, I said it first." She called on Valentina, who said, "A snail, and it's slow." When the next picture came up, Javier's hand shot up, and he kept himself on his chair.

qa.q: What picture did Senora Ruiz hold up first?
qa.a: A picture of a snail.

qa.q: Why did Javier kick the table leg?
qa.a: He felt it was unfair because he had said the answer first, and he was cross at being asked to sit and wait.

qa.q: What could Senora Ruiz try to help children like Javier wait their turn?
qa.a: Give a quiet signal, like a thumb on the chest when they know the answer, and notice the first child who waits.

qa.q: How might Valentina experience Javier's shouting?
qa.a: She may feel her patient waiting goes unnoticed, so it matters that the teacher still chose her.

grounding: It contrasts shouting out and sulking with raising a hand and waiting, and shows a child starting to adopt the habit.

passage: Library period started with the children in a circle on the mat. The librarian said each one could choose a book in turn. Yash, five, jumped up and grabbed the dinosaur book from the shelf. "Mine first!" When she asked him to sit, he threw himself down, shouting, "No! No circle!" Sahil sat cross-legged, waiting, hands in his lap, though his eyes stayed on the dinosaurs. The librarian knelt by Yash and spoke softly. After a minute Yash put the book back on the shelf and sat, still sulking, beside Sahil.

qa.q: Which book did Yash grab?
qa.a: He grabbed the dinosaur book.

qa.q: What might Sahil have been thinking while his eyes stayed on the dinosaurs?
qa.a: He probably wanted the dinosaur book too but waited patiently, hopeful that his turn would come.

qa.q: What went well in how the librarian handled Yash?
qa.a: She knelt and spoke softly instead of shouting, which helped him calm down and rejoin the circle.

qa.q: If you were Sahil, what would you want the librarian to do?
qa.a: Keep the turns fair so waiting pays off, perhaps letting him pick the dinosaur book when his turn comes.

grounding: It contrasts a child's refusal and outburst with another's calm turn-taking during library time.

passage: I'm Chandrika, and on Fridays I help in the kindergarten class where my son studies. Kunal sits at the front table. The first Friday, he tore his worksheet in half and shouted that he hated colouring. This Friday he sat on his chair for the whole story, only wriggling a little. When the teacher asked a question, he raised his hand, pulled it down, then raised it again. He waited until she said his name. I don't know what changed for him, but afterwards he looked round at me, as if to check I had seen.

qa.q: What did Kunal do on the first Friday?
qa.a: He tore his worksheet in half and shouted that he hated colouring.

qa.q: What does Kunal looking round at Chandrika suggest?
qa.a: He may have felt proud of waiting and wanted a grown-up to notice his effort.

qa.q: How could Chandrika respond when he looks round?
qa.a: Give him a small smile or a thumbs up, so he knows his calm waiting was seen. 👍

qa.q: Why can't Chandrika be sure what changed for Kunal?
qa.a: She only helps on Fridays and sees his behaviour, not what happened at home or in class the rest of the week.

grounding: It shows, through a parent helper's eyes, a child moving from outbursts to sitting and raising his hand.

passage:
First week: when Harsha Ma'am asked a question, Santosh jumped up and shouted the answer, pushing past others.
Two weeks later, he raised his hand but called out at the same time. 'Hand up, voice off,' she smiled.
A month on, Santosh sat on his mat, hand stretched high, lips pressed together, bouncing a little. When she called his name, he grinned and answered.

qa.q: What did Santosh do in the first week when a question was asked?
qa.a: He jumped up, shouted the answer and pushed past others.

qa.q: What does Santosh bouncing with his lips pressed together suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was eager to answer but working hard to control himself and wait his turn.

qa.q: What helped Santosh adopt the classroom habit?
qa.a: Harsha Ma'am's short, friendly reminder 'hand up, voice off' gave him a clear rule to practise over time.

qa.q: How might the other children feel about Santosh's change?
qa.a: They may find class calmer and fairer, since they also get a chance to answer.

grounding: Illustrates a young child moving from disruptive outbursts toward classroom etiquette over weeks.

passage: Rain hammered the tin roof of the classroom, and their usual teacher was away. The new teacher had to shout. Tejas climbed under the table and refused to come out. 'I don't want to!' Hemant covered his ears but stayed on his bench, hand up, waiting. When his turn came, he shouted his answer over the rain. The teacher gave him a thumbs up and knelt to talk to Tejas.

qa.q: Why did the new teacher have to shout?
qa.a: Rain was hammering the tin roof, and it was very noisy.

qa.q: What might Tejas have been feeling under the table?
qa.a: He may have felt overwhelmed by the noise and a new teacher, so he refused to cooperate.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Tejas join in?
qa.a: She could speak to him quietly, give him a simple job like handing out books, and invite him back without shaming him.

qa.q: How does Hemant's day differ from Tejas's?
qa.a: Hemant copes with the noise by staying seated and waiting his turn, while Tejas hides and refuses, so their mornings go very differently.

grounding: Shows the contrast between classroom etiquette and refusal to cooperate under noisy, unfamiliar conditions.

passage: In the Bengaluru kindergarten, Rukmini, the teacher, asked, "Who knows what colour a banana is?" Reena, five, jumped up and shouted, "Yellow! Yellow!" before anyone else could speak. Rukmini smiled. "Reena, can you show me your hand?" Reena sat down and put her hand up, wiggling her fingers. Rukmini waited a moment, then said, "Yes, Reena?" "Yellow," Reena said, very proudly.

qa.q: What did Rukmini ask about?
qa.a: What colour a banana is.

qa.q: What does Reena wiggling her fingers suggest?
qa.a: She was bursting with eagerness to answer and found waiting hard.

qa.q: Which choice by Rukmini worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Reena to show her hand, calmly, taught her the class habit without shaming her.

qa.q: How might the other children feel when Reena waits to be called?
qa.a: They might feel they also get a chance, since answers aren't shouted over them.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to raise her hand and wait instead of shouting out in class.

passage:
"How was school, Tejas?" asked his father Joseph.
"Bad. Ma'am made me sit on the mat."
"Why?"
"I didn't want to. I kicked the blocks."
"Hmm. What happened after that?"
"She said, 'Tejas, you can sit or stand quietly at the back.' I sat."
"And?"
"I sat for a whole story. And then I got to hold the book."
Joseph smiled. "Sitting for a story is hard work."
"Very hard. My legs wanted to run."

qa.q: What did Tejas kick?
qa.a: The blocks.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel about sitting on the mat?
qa.a: He found it frustrating and hard, since his legs "wanted to run".

qa.q: What did the teacher do well, and what could Joseph add at home?
qa.a: She gave him a clear choice instead of a fight; Joseph could practise short "sit and listen" times at home.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Tejas sitting for the whole story?
qa.a: She would probably be pleased and use holding the book as a reward.

grounding: Shows a young child moving from a disruptive outburst to sitting for a story, talking it over with his father.

passage:
Teacher's note from Ritu, Friday
Nitin (5) had a much better week. He waited in line at the tap without pushing and raised his hand twice at circle time. On Thursday he got upset when another child took his place on the mat and shouted, "Mine!" I asked him to take three breaths, and he sat next to the other child instead. I'll tell his parents about the hand-raising and the breaths.

qa.q: How many times did Nitin raise his hand at circle time?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when he shouted "Mine!"?
qa.a: He was upset and angry that another child had taken his place.

qa.q: Why is telling Nitin's parents a good idea?
qa.a: They can praise him at home too, which helps the new habits stick.

qa.q: How might the other child on the mat see Nitin's choice to sit beside them?
qa.a: They might feel relieved that there was no fight over the place.

grounding: Shows a young child taking turns and raising his hand in class, with one outburst he recovers from.

passage: In the Kudal anganwadi, the children sat on a mat. Didi held up a picture of a cow. "Who knows what it gives us?" Dilnaz shouted "Milk!" before anyone else, then banged the floor. Salma raised her hand high and wiggled her fingers, lips pressed shut. Didi smiled at her. "Salma?" "Milk and curd," Salma said. Dilnaz shouted again. Didi said gently, "Dilnaz, hand up, like Salma." Dilnaz scowled, then put up her hand, just a little.

qa.q: What picture did Didi hold up?
qa.a: A picture of a cow.

qa.q: What does Salma pressing her lips shut while raising her hand suggest?
qa.a: She was eager to answer but wanted to follow the rule, so she was holding the words in.

qa.q: How did Didi help Dilnaz without scolding?
qa.a: She calmly reminded Dilnaz to raise her hand, pointing to Salma as an example.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt when Salma was chosen?
qa.a: She may have felt annoyed and a bit left out, since she had already shouted the answer.

grounding: In a village anganwadi, one child raises her hand patiently while another shouts out.

passage: Snow had closed the playground, so Class R stayed in for circle time in Leeds. Mrs Clarke passed round the talking stone. "Only the one holding it speaks." Hiroshi held it carefully and told everyone about his snowman. Abebe called out, "Mine was bigger!" and rolled onto his back, kicking. "Abebe, it's Hiroshi's turn." Abebe kicked harder. Mrs Clarke moved beside him and said quietly, "The stone comes to you next." Abebe sat up, arms folded, and waited, staring at the stone.

qa.q: What did Mrs Clarke pass round at circle time?
qa.a: The talking stone.

qa.q: What does Abebe kicking harder after being reminded suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt frustrated and impatient about waiting for his turn to share.

qa.q: What did Mrs Clarke do that helped Abebe settle?
qa.a: She moved close, spoke quietly, and told him he would have the stone next.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi have felt when Abebe called out during his turn?
qa.a: Hiroshi may have felt interrupted, perhaps a little hurt that his snowman story was cut off.

grounding: On a snowy day, one reception child takes his turn with a talking stone while another calls out and kicks.

passage: The Pongal week kolams were chalked on the classroom floor. Kashish sat still on the mat with her hands folded. Lakshmi would not sit. She threw a crayon and yelled, "No story!" The teacher, Mrs Pillai, knelt to her level. "You can stand by the window and listen, or sit next to Kashish." Lakshmi stamped once, then sat beside Kashish, not quite touching the mat. By the end of the story she was leaning on Kashish's arm, listening.

qa.q: What had been chalked on the classroom floor?
qa.a: The Pongal week kolams.

qa.q: Why might Lakshmi have yelled "No story!" and thrown a crayon?
qa.a: She may have felt unsettled or cross about having to sit still, and showed it by refusing.

qa.q: What worked in Mrs Pillai's response?
qa.a: She knelt to Lakshmi's level and offered two acceptable choices instead of a battle.

qa.q: How might Kashish have experienced Lakshmi's outburst and then leaning on her?
qa.a: Kashish may have felt startled at first, then trusted, as Lakshmi calmed down beside her.

grounding: During Pongal week, one child sits still while another throws a crayon, then settles when offered choices.

passage:
I'm Mridul. My little brother Yogesh, five, started school again after the summer holidays. On the first day, I peeked into his classroom.

The teacher asked, "Who knows what colour the sky is?"

Last year Yogesh would have shouted. This time he put his hand up high and wiggled it, lips pressed together.

The teacher picked him. "Blue!" he said. I think he was trying really hard. His hand was still shaking a bit.

qa.q: What did the teacher ask?
qa.a: The teacher asked, "Who knows what colour the sky is?"

qa.q: What might Yogesh have been feeling while he waited with his hand up?
qa.a: Yogesh seemed eager and excited, trying hard to wait his turn instead of shouting.

qa.q: How can the teacher support Yogesh's new habit?
qa.a: The teacher can notice and praise him for raising his hand and waiting.

qa.q: How does Mridul see Yogesh's change?
qa.a: Mridul notices the change from last year and seems proud of how hard Yogesh was trying.

grounding: An older brother observes his little brother raising his hand instead of shouting on the first school day after summer.

passage:
First week of monsoon term: Jahnavi, five, shouts answers, won't sit in the circle, and throws her crayons when told to wait. Jagdish Sir stays calm.

Third week: she sits in the circle but calls out once. Jagdish Sir says, "Hand up, please," and she slowly raises it.

Sixth week: she raises her hand, waits for her turn, and gives her answer. She smiles.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi throw in the first week?
qa.a: She threw her crayons.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel in the sixth week when she gave her answer?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt proud and happy, smiling after waiting her turn.

qa.q: How did Jagdish Sir help Jahnavi learn classroom habits?
qa.a: He stayed calm, gave clear reminders, and let her practise week after week.

qa.q: How might the other children feel as Jahnavi learns to wait?
qa.a: They might feel calmer and get more turns themselves.

grounding: Across the monsoon term, a young child moves from outbursts to raising her hand and taking turns.

passage:
Annual Day rehearsal was chaos. Drums, a microphone squealing, and forty children in costumes in one hall.

Bhavna Ma'am said, "Sit on your spot and wait for your turn."

Preeti, five, sat on her taped star on the floor. The boy next to her was rolling around. She pressed her hands together and watched the stage.

When her group was called, she stood up at once. Bhavna Ma'am gave her a thumbs up.

qa.q: Where did Preeti sit?
qa.a: She sat on her taped star on the floor.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel in the noisy hall?
qa.a: Preeti was probably excited and a little restless, but focused on waiting her turn.

qa.q: How can Bhavna Ma'am help children wait in busy places?
qa.a: She can give each child a clear spot and praise those who wait, like Preeti.

qa.q: How might the boy next to Preeti see her?
qa.a: The boy might see her as calm or wish he could sit still too.

grounding: During a noisy Annual Day rehearsal, a young child sits still and waits her turn.

passage: It was the first rainy week of the new term at a school in Hyderabad. Every time Miss Rukhsana asked a question, Jatin shouted the answer before anyone else could. "Seven! Blue! Elephant!" Asif, beside him, kept his hand up and sighed. On Thursday Miss Rukhsana gave each child a paper leaf. "Hold up your leaf when you know." Jatin's leaf shot up. He bounced in his seat, lips pressed shut. "Jatin?" "Monsoon!" he said, and beamed. Asif got the next turn and grinned at him.

qa.q: What did Miss Rukhsana give each child on Thursday?
qa.a: She gave each child a paper leaf.

qa.q: What does Jatin bouncing with his lips pressed shut suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was excited and eager to answer but trying hard to wait for his turn.

qa.q: What worked in Miss Rukhsana's approach, and why?
qa.a: The paper leaf gave Jatin something to do with his eagerness, so he could wait and still show he knew.

qa.q: What is it like for Asif when Jatin keeps shouting answers?
qa.a: Asif feels frustrated and left out, since a raised hand never gets a turn.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to wait his turn to answer in class instead of shouting out.
